messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 68-year-old South Asian man with a history of divorce and currently working at a non-profit organization, has been struggling since he was raped several months ago. The event itself left him feeling violated and profoundly shaken. He had come to believe that his reactions since the traumatic incident show that he is a lousy coper, leading to a pervasive sense that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again. This belief of being an outsider now has only deepened as time goes on. Ravi’s experience with intrusions and memories has been particularly distressing. When the memory returns, he feels physical pain in the same parts of his body where he was hurt during the event. He sometimes hears things in his head that he heard during the frightening episode, and this auditory recall can leave him feeling disoriented and frightened. The vividness of these memories often leaves Ravi unable to find words to describe what happened, reinforcing his belief that he is a bad coper. These intrusive thoughts and memories have led to various maladaptive strategies as coping mechanisms. He has hurt himself physically to release overwhelming feelings, believing it’s the only way to manage the intensity of the emotions associated with these memories. Moreover, Ravi avoids being alone in a room or building because he fears that being isolated increases his vulnerability. Ravi is always sitting with his back against a wall so he can see everything happening around him. This constant vigilance has made him more reactive and sensitive to potential threats. He reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly, and the sounds of doors closing or creaking floors can trigger intense anxiety. Ravi listens for any signs that might indicate someone is entering his home, perpetuating a cycle of hypervigilance. The cumulative effect of these maladaptive strategies has only reinforced his negative appraisals and heightened sense of threat. Each time he hurts himself physically to cope with the overwhelming emotions, it reinforces his belief that he is an outsider now, incapable of normal emotional responses or healthy coping mechanisms. This self-harm also leads to more frequent intrusions, as the physical pain serves as a reminder of what happened. His fear and hypervigilance have made it difficult for him to interact with others in the non-profit environment where he works. Ravi is often distracted by his need to monitor sounds or his discomfort at being touched unexpectedly, leading to conflicts and misunderstandings with colleagues who do not understand why he reacts so strongly to seemingly minor stimuli. Ravi’s maladaptive strategies have also exacerbated his negative appraisals and threat perception. The physical pain from self-harm reminds him of the original trauma, making it harder for him to believe that life will ever return to normal. Each instance where Ravi feels isolated or startsledd by unexpected touch reinforces his belief that he is an outsider who cannot navigate social interactions safely. These cycles have been escalating over time, and what finally brought Ravi to seek help was the realization that these maladaptive behaviors were only worsening his condition. He is most afraid of never being able to regain a sense of normalcy or feel emotionally whole again. Despite his fears, he hopes therapy can provide him with tools to manage his intrusive thoughts, reduce his hypervigilance, and ultimately help him reconnect with the world around him without feeling like an outsider.
